claim.pdf_says: When an operand is textually subscripted, as operand-j_n (n printed as a subscript), the term 'operand-j' identifies a specific operand and 'n' refers to the nth position or occurrence of operand-j.
claim.markdown_says: When an operand is textually subscripted, as operand-jn, the term 'operand-j' identifies a specific operand and 'n' refers to the nth position or occurrence of operand-j.
claim.why_it_matters: The clause defines the textual-subscript notation itself, and the subscript n was flattened onto the baseline, so the example reads as a term named 'operand-jn' and no longer shows the notation it defines.

verdict.reasoning: Rendered page 51 (printed page 27, §2014:5.4.1) at 300 dpi: the example is printed as 'operand-j' followed by a lowered, smaller 'n' (a true subscript). page-51.md line 9 reads 'as operand-jn' on the baseline. Both sources are quoted accurately. This is not mere styling: §2014:5.4.1 exists to define the subscript notation, and the subscript is the only thing that distinguishes 'operand-j sub n' from a term literally named 'operand-jn'. The surrounding prose still names 'operand-j' and 'n' separately, so a careful reader can recover the intent, which keeps the severity structural rather than normative; the defect is a lost notation mark, not lost rule text.
